passages.title: The watershed map
passages.text:
The flood-control map used by Nandipur’s engineers ended at the municipal boundary. Water did not. After heavy rain, runoff from the market district crossed into a railway settlement whose narrow lanes were absent from the official drainage model. A road was raised to protect the market, but the raised surface redirected water towards the settlement. The project was declared complete because the monitored road remained dry. Residents described a different outcome: more water entered their courtyards, and a shallow well became unusable for several days.

A university team proposed measuring the whole catchment rather than the road named in the contract. It mapped roof drains, informal channels, low points and places where residents already stored rainwater. The exercise uncovered a buried channel that had once carried water towards a wetland. Reopening it was not straightforward. Some sections had been built over, and the wetland itself had become a dumping ground. The team proposed a staged plan: clear a limited section, test water quality, create a planted holding area on public land and measure flow before expanding.

The engineering department objected that infiltration could carry contaminants into groundwater. The residents’ group also warned that a planted basin could become unsafe if it was not maintained. Neither objection was dismissed. The design separated locations suitable for infiltration from those requiring sealed storage, and the municipal budget assigned named staff to inspect the basin after major rainfall. Residents were invited to report blockages, but they were not made responsible for repairs requiring public equipment.

The pilot was not judged by the number of trees planted or photographs taken at its launch. Engineers compared peak water levels at three points, while an independent college recorded whether households in the lowest lanes experienced fewer days of indoor flooding. The first season produced mixed results: the market road improved, but one downstream drain still overflowed. The team published the result and changed the second phase rather than declaring success.

The case illustrates why infrastructure must be evaluated at the scale of the system it changes. A project can reduce risk in one location while exporting it to another. Catchment-wide measurement does not guarantee agreement about every trade-off, but it makes the trade-off visible. It also changes who counts as an informed participant: residents who experience downstream effects become evidence-holders, not merely recipients of instructions.

passages.title: The catalogue and the voice of the clerk
passages.text:
A regional archive began digitising petitions sent to a princely court during a famine. The first task appeared mechanical: flatten fragile paper, photograph each page, attach a date and place, and make the images searchable. The catalogue, however, copied the headings used by the court clerks. A tenant farmer’s complaint appeared under “revenue irregularity”; a widow’s request for grain was listed as “household dependency”. The documents had become easier to find, but the administration’s vocabulary now shaped the first impression a researcher received of the people who had written them.

Archivists disagreed about whether the old headings should be replaced. Some favoured modern terms that described the subject in language readers would understand. Others argued that deleting the original category would conceal how the court had classified disputes and claimants. The archive adopted a dual approach. The original heading remains visible as a quoted archival label, while a separate subject term is added with a note explaining who assigned it. A researcher can search either category and can see that the labels come from different times and purposes.

A second difficulty arose when optical character recognition converted faded handwriting into searchable text. The software confused names, village spellings and quantities. An error could make a document disappear from a search even though its image remained online. The archive now displays machine text as an aid, not as an authoritative transcript. Corrections are logged, uncertain words are marked, and the page image remains available beside the transcription. This is slower than silently replacing every uncertain character, but it preserves evidence of where interpretation has occurred.

Digitisation also changes the context in which a document travels. A cropped image may be shared without its file number or the pages that qualify a statement. Each item therefore carries a provenance note describing the physical collection, the copying process and any limits on reuse. The note cannot stop a misleading quotation, but it gives later readers a way to trace the copy and distinguish the historic document from a modern catalogue description.

The archive’s experience complicates the claim that technology simply makes old information accessible. Labels, search terms and transcription decisions influence what readers notice. Yet refusing digitisation would leave fragile records available mainly to people able to visit the archive. A more defensible practice does not pretend to be neutral. It makes editorial choices visible, preserves the original image and allows later correction without erasing the history of earlier interpretation.

passages.title: The school timetable as an allocation of opportunity
passages.text:
At a government secondary school near a growing city, the timetable was treated as an internal administrative document. When a second language laboratory opened, the head teacher scheduled sessions during the only period when several students travelled home to care for younger siblings. Attendance fell. The first explanation was lack of motivation, because the register showed repeated absences. A teacher asked students to map the hours they spent travelling, caring and studying. Their accounts revealed that the timetable assumed every student’s afternoon was equally available.

The school changed the arrangement without abandoning the laboratory. Sessions were rotated and a supervised study period was offered before the late bus. The change required a revised duty roster and a modest transport payment. It also forced staff to reconsider attendance as a measure of participation. A student arriving late after completing a care task was not necessarily disengaged; a student sitting in the room was not necessarily learning. The school began looking at completed exercises, participation and student feedback alongside the register.

Some teachers feared that responding to individual circumstances would make the timetable unmanageable. The head teacher agreed that common rules were necessary. The issue was whether a rule served an educational purpose or merely simplified administration. The rotation was limited to specified classes, reviewed each term and governed by a published process for requesting changes. Students could not demand any period they preferred, but the school had to explain why a request could not reasonably be accommodated.

The exercise changed the staff’s understanding of fairness. Identical treatment had meant placing every class in the same pattern. Fair access sometimes required a different arrangement so that students facing different constraints could use the same facility. This did not mean every difficulty could be solved by the school. A shortage of buses, for instance, required cooperation with the transport authority rather than another classroom adjustment.

The school’s experience suggests that administrative efficiency should be judged against the purpose of the institution. A timetable is not neutral merely because it is printed in the same format for everyone. It allocates scarce time, determines who can use a resource and can turn an unseen assumption into an attendance penalty. The better rule is not the one with no exceptions; it is the one whose exceptions are reasoned, limited and reviewable.

passages.title: Repairability is not permission to ignore safety
passages.text:
A cooperative of appliance repairers in Surat noticed that customers increasingly arrived with devices that could not be opened without proprietary tools or software authorisation. The cooperative did not argue that every product should be repairable by any person. Batteries can be hazardous, calibration may require specialised equipment and a poorly repaired electrical component can cause a fire. Its complaint was narrower: manufacturers were treating ordinary replacement of a screen or charging port as a security risk even when the work could be performed safely by a trained technician.

The cooperative collected examples of devices discarded because a low-cost part was unavailable outside the manufacturer’s service network. It compared the price of the part, labour and the cost of a replacement device. The figures were not uniform; some products were sensible to repair, while others were not. The recurring problem was that a consumer could not tell whether a repair was impossible, unsafe or merely unauthorised. That uncertainty weakened the customer’s ability to make an informed choice.

A manufacturers’ association replied that unrestricted parts and diagnostic access could expose personal data and undermine product warranties. The cooperative accepted that access needed safeguards. It proposed authenticated diagnostic tools, clear safety instructions and a record of who performed a repair. It also supported restrictions on components whose failure could create a serious hazard. The disagreement shifted from whether access should exist to which tasks required which level of skill and verification.

The debate has consequences beyond household budgets. Repair businesses train apprentices, preserve local technical knowledge and reduce discarded equipment. Yet a repair market cannot be sustained by asking consumers to act responsibly while withholding the parts and information needed to do so. Equally, a right to repair is not a licence to bypass security controls or ignore electrical standards. The useful question is whether a restriction is tied to a demonstrable risk and whether a less restrictive safeguard is available.

The cooperative’s proposal asks for information, not immunity from responsibility. A customer should know the likely cost, risks and effect on warranty before choosing a repair. A technician should have access proportionate to the task and should be accountable for the work performed. Repairability is thus a question of informed choice and calibrated access, not an absolute contest between manufacturers and consumers.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion best expresses the passage’s central argument? (Passage: “The watershed map”)

options.text: Flood-control projects should be assessed across the whole catchment, including people affected downstream.
A project succeeds whenever the road named in its contract remains dry.
Natural drainage should replace all engineered structures.
Residents should be made responsible for maintaining public infrastructure.

questions.explanation: The passage contrasts a narrow site-specific measure with catchment-level outcomes and shared responsibility.

questions.prompt: What did the university team discover by mapping informal channels? (Passage: “The watershed map”)

options.text: The railway settlement had no history of flooding.
A buried channel had once carried water towards a wetland.
The market district received less rainfall than the rest of the city.
Groundwater was safe for unrestricted infiltration.

questions.explanation: The mapping identified a former channel and a degraded wetland, changing the design options.

questions.prompt: Why was the pilot staged rather than expanded immediately? (Passage: “The watershed map”)

options.text: The municipality had decided planted areas were always unsafe.
The team wanted to avoid measuring downstream effects.
The channel, water quality and maintenance arrangements required testing before wider work.
Residents opposed every form of drainage improvement.

questions.explanation: The text identifies uncertainties about built-over sections, contamination and maintenance.

questions.prompt: Which additional finding would most strongly support expansion? (Passage: “The watershed map”)

options.text: The market road remained dry during one light shower.
The launch attracted more visitors than the previous year’s event.
The number of trees planted exceeded the initial target.
Seasonal measurements show lower peak levels without increased flooding in downstream homes.

questions.explanation: The evaluation requires catchment-level evidence, not publicity or one-site performance.

questions.prompt: The phrase “exporting risk” refers to: (Passage: “The watershed map”)

options.text: reducing danger in one place by shifting its burden to another location.
selling flood-control technology to another municipality.
moving residents to a different district after rainfall.
measuring water levels outside the catchment.

questions.explanation: The passage uses the phrase for downstream flooding caused by the raised road.

questions.prompt: Which implementation choice follows the author’s reasoning? (Passage: “The watershed map”)

options.text: Declare success once the market road remains dry.
Publish mixed results, revise the second phase and monitor effects across the catchment.
Remove residents from monitoring because only engineers hold relevant evidence.
Expand infiltration uniformly despite groundwater warnings.

questions.explanation: The author supports transparent evaluation and adaptation rather than a universal intervention.

questions.prompt: Which tension drives the archive’s decision to retain original labels and add modern ones? (Passage: “The catalogue and the voice of the clerk”)

options.text: Deciding whether petitions should be treated as court judgments.
Choosing between physical storage and digital photography.
Preserving evidence of the court’s categories while making records intelligible to present-day researchers.
Preventing researchers from searching by subject.

questions.explanation: The dual catalogue preserves historical terminology while adding a separately attributed descriptive layer.

questions.prompt: Why does the archive keep the page image beside the machine transcription? (Passage: “The catalogue and the voice of the clerk”)

options.text: The image is needed only to prove that the paper was old.
The software cannot display more than one page at a time.
The archive intends to eliminate human correction.
Recognition errors can alter names, places and quantities, so the image remains the reference record.

questions.explanation: The passage gives OCR-error examples and explains that uncertain readings must remain traceable.

questions.prompt: What is the principal purpose of the provenance note? (Passage: “The catalogue and the voice of the clerk”)

options.text: To record the source collection, copying process and restrictions so that a digital item can be traced.
To certify every allegation in the petition as factually true.
To replace the historic file number with a modern title.
To prevent all later users from quoting the document.

questions.explanation: The note supplies context for the copy; it does not independently verify the petitioner’s claims.

questions.prompt: Which assumption does the final paragraph reject? (Passage: “The catalogue and the voice of the clerk”)

options.text: That remote access can widen participation.
That digitisation is a purely mechanical process without interpretive choices.
That historical categories may reflect institutional priorities.
That fragile paper requires preservation.

questions.explanation: The conclusion names labels, search terms and transcription as choices that affect visibility.

questions.prompt: Which feature would best extend the archive’s method? (Passage: “The catalogue and the voice of the clerk”)

options.text: A search function hiding original headings once a modern term is added.
A system that silently overwrites every uncertain word with the most common spelling.
A public correction log showing the earlier reading, revised reading and reason for the change.
A catalogue ranking documents only by download count.

questions.explanation: The archive values visible correction and preservation of interpretive history.

questions.prompt: The author’s attitude towards digitisation is best described as: (Passage: “The catalogue and the voice of the clerk”)

options.text: indifferent because catalogue choices do not affect research.
unreservedly celebratory because searchable text is always accurate.
hostile because digital copies cannot preserve historical evidence.
supportive but alert to the interpretive and contextual risks it creates.

questions.explanation: The passage recognises wider access while explaining why digital records need safeguards.

questions.prompt: What prompted the school to reconsider its original timetable? (Passage: “The school timetable as an allocation of opportunity”)

options.text: Student accounts showed that the schedule ignored unequal caring and travel responsibilities.
The laboratory equipment was defective.
The school had more teachers than classrooms.
The transport authority ordered the school to end language teaching.

questions.explanation: Students’ time maps revealed why the register alone gave a misleading picture of engagement.

questions.prompt: Which distinction does the passage draw between presence and learning? (Passage: “The school timetable as an allocation of opportunity”)

options.text: A late arrival must always be treated as a complete absence.
A register entry cannot by itself establish whether a student has engaged with the lesson.
Completed exercises are irrelevant to evaluating a timetable.
Learning can be measured only through laboratory attendance.

questions.explanation: The school broadened evaluation to participation, exercises and feedback.

questions.prompt: Why was the rotation limited and reviewed each term? (Passage: “The school timetable as an allocation of opportunity”)

options.text: To prevent students from ever requesting an adjustment.
To ensure only high-performing students used the laboratory.
To accommodate genuine constraints while keeping common rules workable.
To transfer all scheduling decisions to parents.

questions.explanation: The text balances accommodation with manageability through a defined, reviewable procedure.

questions.prompt: What does the passage suggest about equality and fairness? (Passage: “The school timetable as an allocation of opportunity”)

options.text: A school can eliminate every social difference through scheduling.
Fairness requires every student to choose a separate timetable.
Common rules are inherently unfair and should be abolished.
Identical arrangements may produce unequal access when students face different constraints.

questions.explanation: The example shows that equal access can require a limited adjustment to a common arrangement.

questions.prompt: Which request best fits the school’s published procedure? (Passage: “The school timetable as an allocation of opportunity”)

options.text: A student explains a recurring care-related conflict and asks for a defined alternative session.
A student demands any preferred period without explaining a conflict.
A parent asks the school to suspend classes whenever transport is delayed.
A teacher asks that the review procedure be removed.

questions.explanation: The process permits reasoned, defined requests but not unrestricted personal choice.

questions.prompt: The final paragraph mainly serves to: (Passage: “The school timetable as an allocation of opportunity”)

options.text: argue that attendance records should no longer be maintained.
recast the timetable as an allocation of opportunity rather than a neutral clerical tool.
show that transport shortages can always be solved by changing class periods.
claim that administrative uniformity is harmful in every setting.

questions.explanation: The conclusion links a routine document to access, resource allocation and accountability.

questions.prompt: Which formulation best captures the cooperative’s position? (Passage: “Repairability is not permission to ignore safety”)

options.text: Manufacturers should be prohibited from offering their own repair services.
Every device should be repairable by anyone without tools or training.
Repair access should be proportionate to the task, with safety and security safeguards.
Consumers should be required to repair devices rather than replace them.

questions.explanation: The cooperative accepts safeguards but objects to restrictions unrelated to demonstrated risks.

questions.prompt: What uncertainty most directly weakens a customer’s choice? (Passage: “Repairability is not permission to ignore safety”)

options.text: Not knowing whether the manufacturer advertises online.
Not knowing the colour of the replacement device.
Not knowing the number of apprentices in the city.
Not knowing whether a repair is impossible, unsafe or merely unauthorised.

questions.explanation: The unexplained reason for refusing a repair is the consumer-information problem.

questions.prompt: How does the manufacturers’ association’s response affect the debate? (Passage: “Repairability is not permission to ignore safety”)

options.text: It introduces privacy, warranty and safety concerns that require a calibrated access model.
It establishes that every independent repair causes data theft.
It proves environmental concerns are irrelevant.
It shows that spare parts are never available to manufacturers.

questions.explanation: The response raises legitimate risks, and the cooperative proposes task-specific safeguards.

questions.prompt: Which policy would the author most likely reject? (Passage: “Repairability is not permission to ignore safety”)

options.text: Authenticated diagnostic access for trained technicians.
A blanket prohibition on independent access regardless of the task or evidence of risk.
Safety restrictions for components whose failure may cause serious harm.
Clear pre-repair disclosure of cost and warranty implications.

questions.explanation: The passage objects to restrictions not connected to demonstrable risk.

questions.prompt: The phrase “calibrated access” refers to: (Passage: “Repairability is not permission to ignore safety”)

options.text: a guarantee that every repair will cost the same amount.
the use of a measuring instrument to test battery voltage.
levels of information and tool access matched to the skill and risk of a repair.
the removal of all manufacturer-controlled software.

questions.explanation: The phrase summarises the proposal for authenticated tools and task-specific safeguards.

questions.prompt: Which additional evidence would most strengthen the cooperative’s case? (Passage: “Repairability is not permission to ignore safety”)

options.text: A record of the cooperative’s social-media followers.
A list of the most popular appliance colours sold in the city.
A survey of customers’ favourite packaging designs.
A comparison showing how often common repairs are refused despite low safety risk and trained technicians being available.

questions.explanation: Evidence about refusals and actual risk directly tests the claimed restriction.
